quote: A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.
content: Planck’s principle has been tested and is partly true. When a star scientist dies, publications by outsiders in the field rise, citations shift toward newcomers’ ideas, and the effect is concentrated in fields where the star had been a gatekeeper (Azoulay, Fons-Rosen & Graff Zivin (2019)), which is Planck’s mechanism at the level of funding and refereeing. Earlier historical tests found the opposite for the case Planck would have had in mind: older scientists accepted Darwin at rates not much below younger ones (Hull, Tessner & Diamond (1978)). The essay’s gloss, that acceptance of many-worlds is growing as “the pack grows larger,” is not supported by the polls (the annotations on Quantum Explanations give the figures), and its parenthetical example of a field held back by ridiculous objections, evolutionary psychology, is a field whose objectors Book III’s annotations found to have been substantially right. The principle is a decent description of how some ideas spread. It does not tell you which ideas were the truths.

quote: Suppose you came up with some way of generating hypotheses that was completely crazy—say, pumping a robot-controlled Ouija board with the digits of pi—and the resulting suggestions kept on getting verified experimentally. The pure ideal essence of Science wouldn’t skip a beat. The pure ideal essence of Bayes would burst into flames and die.
content: Bayes would do nothing of the kind. The distinction between the context of discovery and the context of justification (Reichenbach, 1938) is precisely the point that the origin of a hypothesis is irrelevant to its confirmation, and Bayes’s theorem is a rule of justification: it takes a hypothesis and evidence and returns a posterior, with no term for where the hypothesis came from. A Bayesian who observed the Ouija board’s suggestions being verified would update toward “the Ouija board is a reliable source,” exactly as they would for any instrument with a track record, and would feel no flames. What would be threatened is the essay’s thermodynamic thesis from The Second Law and Engines of Cognition, that generating a true hypothesis requires prior evidence-work, and that thesis is not Bayes; it is a claim about the physics of inference that the annotations on those essays found to be decoration. The essay’s real point, that in a large hypothesis space most of the evidential work is in locating the hypothesis, is right and is Book I’s Einstein’s Arrogance; the human process that does the locating is heuristic (analogy, symmetry, the character of previous laws), which is what Simon and Langley’s BACON program showed by rediscovering Kepler’s third law from tables (Langley et al., Scientific Discovery, 1987). Neither Science nor Bayes cares about the Ouija board; only the thermodynamic essays do, and they are wrong.
